The East Harbor Seawall is a reinforced concrete structure protecting the eastern waterfront of Northport from storm surge and wave action.

Early history

Before the wall was built, the harbor district flooded several times each decade, and the fishing fleet often moved upriver for the winter to avoid damage.

Planning began in 1972 after a storm pushed water three blocks inland. The original design was revised twice to account for updated wave height estimates.

Design and construction

The wall consists of interlocking concrete panels anchored to steel piles driven twelve meters into the harbor floor. A curved parapet deflects spray away from the promenade.

Construction was completed in 1978 at a cost of 14 million dollars, considerably more than the initial estimate, mostly due to the discovery of unstable sediment.

Later restoration

Inspections in 2019 found spalling concrete and exposed rebar along a 300 meter section, prompting a partial closure of the promenade for emergency repairs.

A full replacement was approved in 2024, and the new wall is expected to remain in service for at least fifty years under current sea level projections.
